main_damage_causes: Harry's agency and heroism are amplified and aestheticized (statue climb, bold descent on the basilisk) at the expense of the book's theme that desperate, faithful surrender — not spectacular initiative — is what summons aid and defines Gryffindor courage
The Ron-Hermione emotional bond is subtly deprioritized in the reunion scene in favor of Harry-Hermione centrality, a pattern with cumulative consequences across the saga
The basilisk's role as an instrument of near-hopeless terror is softened by compressing and choreographing the combat, reducing the psychological and physical cost the encounter imposes on Harry

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (CoS) - Chamber of Secrets: Harry climbs the Slytherin statue to retrieve the sword
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 24-25: The basilisk sweeps the Sorting Hat into Harry's arms while he is on the floor, cornered; Harry puts the hat on while lying flat and pleads mentally 'Help me - help me - Harry thought, his eyes screwed tight under the hat. Please help me.' The sword arrives while Harry is prostrate and desperate.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Harry sees the Sorting Hat already in the chamber (dropped by Fawkes), then proactively climbs the statue of Slytherin himself and retrieves the sword from within the hat at the top, acting with bold initiative rather than desperate last-resort supplication.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's moment is defined by Harry's helplessness and the miraculous nature of the sword's arrival answering his silent plea — it is a test of faith and loyalty rewarded. The film turns it into a display of Harry's own initiative and daring athleticism. Dumbledore's later line 'only a true Gryffindor could have pulled that out of the Hat' retains its surface meaning in both versions, but the emotional and thematic weight — that courage is proven in desperate, faithful surrender, not heroic climbing — is significantly diluted. The scene's function as a demonstration of Dumbledore-given loyalty being rewarded is partially lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (CoS) - Chamber of Secrets: Fawkes blinds the basilisk before Harry fights it
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 22-27: Fawkes blinds the basilisk while Harry is running blindly and in mortal terror, having already tripped and fallen. Harry only turns to fight after the basilisk is blinded, seizing the moment when 'the basilisk's head was falling, its body coiling around.' Harry fights blind alongside a blind snake, navigating by sound and shadow. The combat is terrifying and attritional.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Fawkes blinds the basilisk while Harry watches the shadows on the wall, then Harry climbs the statue and descends upon the basilisk in a described 'mad rush of courage,' sliding down its back — a visually spectacular, more overtly heroic sequence. The film compresses and choreographs the fight into a single bold assault rather than the book's desperate, groping, protracted struggle.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's combat conveys that Harry's victory is agonizing, near-miraculous, and achieved despite terror — he trips, bleeds, and barely survives. The film's version, while retaining the basilisk-fang wound, presents Harry as more controlled and heroic. This softens the portrayal of the basilisk as an existential, almost unbeatable threat and reduces the psychological cost of the encounter on Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (CoS) - Tunnel: Harry destroys the diary with the basilisk fang
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 31: Harry destroys the diary 'without thinking, without considering, as though he had meant to do it all along' — an instinctive, spontaneous act while Riddle is distracted and before Riddle realizes the threat. Harry seizes the fang lying next to him and plunges it into the diary immediately.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Riddle is fully aware and lunges forward to stop Harry, explicitly saying 'What are you doing? No. Stop...' before Harry destroys the diary. Harry also crawls toward Ginny first, takes the diary from her hand, then destroys it — making it a more deliberate, observed action under pressure from a reacting Riddle.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's instinctive, unobserved act carries thematic weight about Harry acting on pure instinct and loyalty. The film version still works dramatically but removes the elegance of Riddle being caught off-guard by Harry's improvisation. Minor damage as the core action and outcome are preserved.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (CoS) - Hospital Wing/Great Hall reunion: Hermione embraces Harry, shakes Ron's hand
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 41: Ron simply says 'So Hermione's okay!' brightly upon learning she will recover. The book does not dramatize the reunion scene at the feast in the way the film does, but the overall dynamic is warm and equal among the trio.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Hermione runs in, embraces Harry first ('You solved it! You solved it!'), then turns to Ron — and they share an awkward pause before shaking hands. Ron says 'Welcome back, Hermione,' stiffly. This is played for comedic awkwardness and implicitly downplays the Ron-Hermione emotional bond at a moment of relief.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film corpus for DH (Book Scenes 48-52) and the broader book corpus establish the Ron-Hermione relationship as the saga's central romantic arc. Having their reunion after Hermione's petrification play as an awkward handshake — versus Harry receiving a full embrace — misrepresents the emotional priority of their bond at this early stage. This is a minor but meaningful early signal that the film slightly subordinates the Ron-Hermione connection to Harry-Hermione centrality, consistent with a pattern across the film series.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (CoS) - Chamber: Riddle explicitly taunts dying Harry at length
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 30: After the fang pierces Harry, the narration focuses on Harry's physical experience — 'White-hot pain was spreading slowly and steadily from the wound' and his vision going foggy. Riddle is present but the book does not give him an extended monologue taunting the dying Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Riddle delivers a substantial taunting monologue over the dying Harry: 'Remarkable, isn't it? How quickly the venom of the Basilisk penetrates the body?... I'd guess you have little more than a minute to live... So ends the famous Harry Potter. On his knees in the Chamber of Secrets. Defeated at last...' This is an extended villain gloat not present in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book focuses on Harry's subjective experience of dying and his determination to destroy the diary; the film shifts focus to Riddle's villainous gloating. This makes Riddle more conventionally theatrical and slightly reduces the interiority of Harry's near-death experience. Damage is minor — Riddle's menace is enhanced if anything — but the adaptation choice shifts the emotional register of the scene away from Harry's perspective.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (CoS) - Chamber: Sorting Hat dropped by Fawkes, then tossed aside by Riddle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 24: 'The basilisk had swept the Sorting Hat into Harry's arms.' The hat arrives mid-battle via the basilisk's own tail accidentally delivering it to Harry, who then puts it on and pleads for help. Riddle does not interact with the hat.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Fawkes carries in and drops the Sorting Hat. Riddle picks it up, mocks it ('This is what Dumbledore sends his defender! A songbird and an old hat!'), then tosses it aside. Harry later retrieves the sword from within it at the top of the statue.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Riddle handling and mocking the hat before discarding it — only for it to save Harry — adds a dramatic irony beat not in the book. More importantly, Riddle's dismissal of the hat removes the element of the basilisk unwittingly delivering salvation to Harry, which in the book reinforces the theme that Voldemort's own actions contribute to his defeat. The film's version is coherent but loses this thematic nuance. Additionally, having Fawkes deliver the hat rather than it arriving chaotically mid-battle removes the sense of desperate miraculous provision.
